case_name: Ramadan v The University of British Columbia
text:
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Ramadan v. The University of British
Columbia,

2018 BCSC 1132

Date:
20180706

Docket:
S094660

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

Ehab
Farouk Mohamed Ramadan

Plaintiff

And:

The
University of British Columbia, the Senate Appeal on Academic Standing,
Enrolment Service/Senate & Curriculum Services of the University of British
Columbia, the Faculty of Graduate Studies of the University of British
Columbia, the Department of Anesthesia, Pharmacology & Therapeutics of UBC

Defendants

Corrected
Judgment:  The text of the judgment was corrected at paragraph 51 on
July 31, 2018.

Before:
The Honourable Mr. Justice D.M. Masuhara

Reasons for Judgment

In Chambers

Acting on his own behalf:

E.F.M.
Ramadan

Counsel for the Defendants:

L.
Tsang

Place and Dates of Hearing:

Vancouver,
B.C.

June
13, 2018

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

July
6, 2018

I.

introduction

[
1
]

This is an application to dismiss a variety of
claims arising out of the plaintiff’s removal from the PhD program at the
University of British Columbia.  It is the third such application in slightly
less than a decade since this case began.  The prior two applications were
granted with leave to the plaintiff to amend his pleadings.

[
2
]

The defendants say that the defects identified
in the earlier decisions remain.  They ask that the pleadings be struck and
that the plaintiff be prohibited from filing any further claim against them
without leave of the Court.

II.

pleadings chronology

[
3
]

This action began in or around June 2009
when the plaintiff filed a writ of summons.  He filed an amended writ of summons
and a 92-page Statement of Claim on June 18, 2010.

[
4
]

On July 27, 2010, the defendants took the
position that the Statement of Claim was improper because it pled evidence,
argument and included documents.  They encouraged him to seek legal advice.

[
5
]

On July 30, 2010, the plaintiff advised the
defendants that he would amend his pleadings.  Counsel for the defendants again
told the plaintiff his pleadings were improper in a number of ways, encouraged
him to seek legal advice, and advised him that if the pleadings remained
improper, the defendants would bring an application to strike.

[
6
]

On August 17, 2010, the plaintiff requested
an extension so he could seek legal advice and file his pleadings in the new
form (Notice of Civil Claim).  The defendants consented.

[
7
]

On August 19, 2010, the plaintiff delivered
a filed 93-page Notice of Civil Claim and advised the defendants that he had
filed it without any changes and without seeking legal advice.  He then advised
that he would work on amending it.

[
8
]

On October 25, 2010, the plaintiff filed a
172-page Amended Notice of Civil Claim.

[
9
]

On November 25, 2010, counsel for the defendants
told the plaintiff the Amended Notice of Civil Claim was still defective
because it contained needless and vexatious allegations and an action was not
the proper forum for academic disputes.  Counsel told the plaintiff that the defendants
were prepared to provide more time to amend the pleadings, but if it continued
in its current form they would apply to have it struck.

[
10
]

On January 13, 2011, the defendants applied
to have the Amended Notice of Civil Claim struck on the basis that it was
prolix, pled evidence, disclosed no reasonable claim, was unnecessary,
scandalous, frivolous or vexatious, or may prejudice, embarrass or delay the
fair trial or hearing of the proceeding (the “First Application”).

[
11
]

The First Application was heard on January 19,
2011 and Loo J. granted the application with leave to the plaintiff to
amend his pleadings:
Ramadan v. University of British Columbia
(19
January 2011), Vancouver S094660 (S.C.).

Loo J. strongly
encouraged the plaintiff to seek legal advice.

[
12
]

On or about June 10, 2011, the plaintiff
delivered to the defendants an unfiled Amended Notice of Civil Claim.

[
13
]

On June 16, 2011, counsel for the defendants
advised the plaintiff that these pleadings suffered from the same defects as
those Loo J. struck, and advised him to seek legal advice.

[
14
]

On July 14, 2011, the plaintiff filed a
54-page further Amended Notice of Civil Claim (the “Further Amended Claim”).

[
15
]

On July 15, counsel for the defendants told
the plaintiff that the Further Amended Claim was improper and the defendants
would apply to have it struck.

[
16
]

On September 8, 2011, counsel for the defendants
requested the plaintiff to provide him with his available dates to have the defendants’
application to strike heard and that no further steps would be taken until it
was heard.

[
17
]

The plaintiff ignored counsel’s repeated
requested for his availability until April 23, 2012.

[
18
]

On April 25, 2012, counsel for the defendants
advised the plaintiff that the defendants would proceed with scheduling the
application.  Counsel again advised the plaintiff that he should seek legal
advice and that the defendants would agree to delay the application until he
had received legal advice and had a reasonable opportunity to revise his
pleading.

[
19
]

On April 30, 2012, the defendants filed an
application to strike the Further Amended Claim and set the date for December 3,
2012 (the “Second Application”).

[
20
]

On December 3, 2012, Affleck J.
granted the Second Application with costs to the defendants:
Ramadan v. University
of British Columbia
(December 3, 2012), Vancouver S094660 (S.C.).

He
concluded the Further Amended Claim “exhibits the same egregious defects as did
its predecessor”.  In granting leave to amend to the plaintiff, Affleck J.
warned the plaintiff that should there be another successful application, the
Court may conclude that the plaintiff should not be entitled to amend without
first obtaining the Court’s permission.  Affleck J. also strongly
encouraged the plaintiff to seek legal advice.

[
21
]

On February 15, 2013, the plaintiff filed a
20-page second further Amended Notice of Civil Claim (the “Second Further
Amended Claim”).

[
22
]

No further steps were taken in the litigation
other than a few emails exchanged between the plaintiff and counsel for the defendants
in July 2016.

[
23
]

On February 9, 2018, the plaintiff wrote to
counsel for the defendants to seek trial dates.

[
24
]

On February 13, 2018, counsel for the defendants
responded that the plaintiff would need to file and serve a Notice of Intention
to Proceed and advised him to seek legal advice.

[
25
]

On or about February 15, 2018, the plaintiff
delivered and filed a Notice of Intention to Proceed.

[
26
]

On March 22, 2018, counsel for the defendants
advised the plaintiff that the Second Further Amended Claim suffered from the
same defects as the earlier pleadings and that if the plaintiff intended to
proceed they would bring an application to strike.  Counsel further advised
that they would seek an order that he not be permitted to file any claim
against the defendants without leave of the Court.

III.

law

[
27
]

Rule 9-5(1) states:

(1)
At any
stage of a proceeding, the court may order to be struck out or amended the
whole or any part of a pleading, petition or other document on the ground that

(a)
it discloses no reasonable claim
or defence, as the case may be,

(b)
it is unnecessary, scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious,

(c)
it may
prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair trial or hearing of the proceeding, or

(d)
it is
otherwise an abuse of the process of the court,

and the court
may pronounce judgment or order the proceeding to be stayed or dismissed and
may order the costs of the application to be paid as special costs.

[
28
]

The law related to striking pleadings was
summarized in
Sahyoun v. Ho
,
2015 BCSC 392
, appeal dismissed as
abandoned
2017 BCCA 96
, at paras.
57-63
:

[57]      The test on an application to
strike an action under R. 9-5(1)(a), on the basis the pleadings do not
disclose a cause of action, is whether it is plain and obvious the claim cannot
succeed.

It requires a conclusion that, assuming that the facts as
stated are true, those facts disclose no cause of action and the pleadings
disclose no arguable issue.  If there is a chance that the action may succeed,
then the action should be allowed to proceed;
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.
,

1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959 at 980;
Thompson v. Webber
,
2010 BCCA 308
at
para.
11
;
Canadian Bar Assn. v. British Columbia
,
2008 BCCA 92

at para.
37
.

[58]      The test for striking a pleading
under R. 9-5(1)(b), on the basis that it is unnecessary, scandalous,
frivolous or vexatious, was recently summarized in
Willow v. Chong
,
2013
BCSC 1083
, where Fisher J. said:

[20]      Under Rule 9-5(1)(b), a
pleading is unnecessary or vexatious if it does not go to establishing the
plaintiff’s cause of action, if it does not advance any claim known in law,
where it is obvious that an action cannot succeed, or where it would serve no
useful purpose and would be a waste of the court’s time and public resources:
Citizens
for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] BCJ No. 2160
(SC);
Skender v Farley
,
2007 BCCA 629
.

If a pleading is so
confusing that it is difficult to understand what is pleaded, it may also be
unnecessary, frivolous or vexatious.

[59]      An “embarrassing” pleading, as
contemplated by R. 9-5(1)(c), is one that is so irrelevant that to allow it to
stand would involve useless expense and would also prejudice the trial of the
action by involving the parties in a dispute apart from the issues;
Keddie v.
Dumas Hotels Ltd.
(1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 at 147 (C.A.).

[60]      The abuse of process standard
under R. 9-5(1)(d) derives from a flexible doctrine.

It allows the
court to prevent a claim from proceeding where to do so would violate
principles of judicial economy, consistency, finality and the integrity of the
administration of justice;
Toronto (City) v. C.U.P.E., Local 79
,
2003
SCC 63
at paras.
35-37
.

[61]      Though subsections (a)-(d) of R. 9-5(1)
address different concerns and different wrongs, there is also some overlap
between these subsections.

Thus, for example, a pleading that discloses
no cause of action, contrary to R. 9-5(1)(a), can also be unnecessary,
frivolous or vexatious within the meaning of  R. 9-5(1)(b); see e.g.

Virk v. Brar
,
2012 BCSC 1004
at paras.
69-70
.

[62]      A pleading can be embarrassing if
it does not state the real issue in an intelligible form.

It can also
be embarrassing if it is prolix, includes irrelevant facts, argument or
evidence.  It can be prejudicial if it is designed to or has the effect of
confusing the defendant, making it difficult, if not impossible, to answer;
Virk

at para.
75
.

[63]      These
same concerns can constitute an abuse of the court if a litigant has been
expressly told that there are aspects of its pleadings that are deficient or
defective, and if that litigant persists, in its amended claim, to advance the
same claims or issues in the same way

IV.

the parties’ positions

[
29
]

The defendants say that the Second Further
Amended Claim ought to be struck under essentially every subheading of Rule 9-5(1)
of the
Supreme Court Civil Rules
.

[
30
]

The defendants say that there is no reasonable
cause of action because the claims’ essential character is academic, and
therefore they must be dealt with exclusively through the university’s internal
appeal procedures and any subsequent judicial review, citing
Jaffer v. York
University,
2010 ONCA 654
, leave to appeal ref’d 2010 S.C.C.A. No. 402,
and
Dawson v. University of Toronto,
2007 CanLII 4311 (ON SC)
, [2007] O.J. No. 591 (QL)
(S.C.), leave to appeal ref’d
2007 ONCA 875
.

The defendants also
argue that the claims are an abuse of process and constitute a collateral
attack on the decision by the Senate Appeal Committee, in which it decided to
dismiss the plaintiff’s appeal of the decision to remove him from the PhD
program.

[
31
]

The defendants further argue that the Second
Further Amended Claim fails to plead material facts supporting elements of
various causes of action.  For example, the plaintiff pleads the existence of a
contract between him and the University with the terms being “all Policies,
Regulations, Ordinances, the Act of the University, and the Statutes of the
University of British Columbia”, but does not plead any material facts related
to which particular terms have been breached.  Similarly, breach of trust and
defamation are referred to but no material facts related to them are pleaded.

[
32
]

The Second Further Amended Claim is also prolix
and pleads irrelevant facts and evidence, mingling facts and a wide variety of
claims, making it difficult to even understand the case to be met.

[
33
]

Some of the allegations such as the claims of
forgery and fabrication of evidence do not give rise to a claim:
Sahyoun
at
para. 46.  Nor do claims of breaches of the
Human Rights Code,
R.S.B.C.
1996, c. 210 fall within this Court’s jurisdiction.

[
34
]

The defendants repeat the observation of
Donald J.A. in
The Owners, Strata Plan LMS 3259 v. Sze Holding
Inc.
,
2015 BCCA 424
at para.
11
:

[11]      …
Self-represented litigants must understand that the court is not a free fire
zone where anything can be said regardless of the harm to others and their
reputations.

[
35
]

The plaintiff responds that academic disputes
may give rise to civil liability:
Olar v. Laurentian University
,
2007
CanLII 20787
(Ont. S.C.), aff’d
2008 ONCA 699
.  More generally, he says
the claim discloses reasonable causes of action in “fraud, misrepresentation,
harassment, and conspiracy within the laws of duty of care and contract that
the [defendants] breached”, that the Second Further Amended Claim does not fall
within any of the categories of Rule 9-5(1), and that the defendants fail
to point to any particular paragraphs which do so.

V.

analysis

[
36
]

In my view, the “essential character” argument has
some merit, however, it does not appear to be a complete answer here.  For
example, the Court of Appeal has declined to strike claims that related to
academic matters such as inadequate instruction/supervision:
Mohl v. The
University of British Columbia
,
2006 BCCA 70
.  Instead, I rest my decision
on the well settled principles routinely applied in applications to strike, as
set out in
Sahyoun
.  That is to say abuse of process.  The pleadings
should be struck because they constitute an abuse of process, running afoul of
every subsection of Rule 9-5(1).

[
37
]

The most fundamental problem with the Second
Further Amended Claim is that it is so confusingly drafted that it is
impossible to know what facts are intended to support which claim, what causes
of action are actually being pursued, and who is alleged to have committed
which cause of action.  The vast majority of the “particulars” of each claim
are a mixed summary of elements of various different causes of action.

[
38
]

It is impossible to go through each paragraph
with a view to pointing out each error.  However, I will attempt to provide
some illustrations.

[
39
]

The plaintiff organizes his pleadings into nine
claims, but each involves multiple causes of action.  It is difficult to
discern which causes of action the plaintiff has attempted to plead, but they
appear to include negligence, misrepresentation (negligent and fraudulent),
conspiracy and breach of contract.  The elements of each tort are repeatedly
mixed.  As an example, at page 7, the plaintiff says that UBC
“fraudulently reproduced” a report which recommended that he not be permitted
to continue in the PhD program.  There follows a section regarding particulars
of what appears in the main to be a fraudulent misrepresentation claim.  The
particulars include an allegation that “[t]he defendant negligently owed the
plaintiff duty of care and the defendant negligently breached that duty of care
and the contract”.  He subsequently says that the Senate Appeal Committee
“negligently relied on the reproduced false material”.

[
40
]

The plaintiff pleads on page 8 of the Second
Further Amended Claim that he “put trust on the defendant and the defendant
abused and breached the trust”.  There are no material facts plead that would
put the parties in a trust relationship.  Indeed, it appears that the plaintiff
has misconstrued the particular legal meaning of trust and has pleaded that in
a general sense he had confidence or placed reliance on the defendant.  That in
itself does not give rise to a fiduciary relationship.

[
41
]

Under his third claim, he pleads a “negligent
fraudulent misrepresentation”.  In the particulars, he pleads duress, breach of
duty of care and breach of contract, abuse of trust and bad faith.

[
42
]

On page 11 the plaintiff says that a letter
defamed him.  There are no particulars about the allegedly defamatory contents
of the letter.

[
43
]

The plaintiff pleads a number of different
contracts: one with UBC, the terms of which are essentially all laws and
policies which apply to it; two contracts with non-parties for supervision (and
he does not plead that UBC was a party to either); and another agreement that
UBC would allow him to be reinstated to the PhD program if he accepted being
placed in the master’s program.  He pleads that the Regulations and Statutes of
UBC and “the law” were breached, but provides no material facts related to
this.

[
44
]

The plaintiff pleads that a signature on an
important letter was forged.  Forgery in itself is not a cause of action,
though it may be part of a fraudulent misrepresentation.  The elements of the
tort were set out in
Bruno Appliance and Furniture Inc. v. Hryniak
,
2014
SCC 8
at para.
21
:

(1) a false
representation made by the defendant; (2) some level of knowledge of the
falsehood of the representation on the part of the defendant (whether through
knowledge or recklessness); (3) the false representation caused the plaintiff
to act; and (4) the plaintiff’s actions resulted in a loss.

[
45
]

The plaintiff pleads that he relied on the
letter but fails to plead material facts capable of supporting that allegation.

The letter is alleged to have required him to withdraw from the PhD program
or face being removed from the faculty of graduate studies.  There is no
suggestion that he was not in fact faced with this choice – indeed, the plaintiff
pleads repeatedly that he was in fact compelled by multiple people within the
University to make this choice, and the requirement was upheld by the Senate
Appeal Committee.  The plaintiff does not plead any material facts that could
remotely support any causative impact of the signature.  Similarly, the
allegation that the letter contained a “negligent material misrepresentation
about the plaintiff’s progress with his Ph.D. program” – which allegation is
entirely unparticularized – is not accompanied by any material facts capable of
establishing that the plaintiff relied to his detriment on it.

[
46
]

This analysis applies to any alleged negligent
misrepresentation, which also requires detrimental reliance:
Queen v. Cognos
Inc
.,
1993 CanLII 146 (SCC)
, [1993] 1 S.C.R. 87.

[
47
]

Conspiracy is alleged at several points.

The
tort of conspiracy requires proof of an agreement either (1) with the intent to
injure, and injury does in fact result, or (2) to employ unlawful means
directed at the plaintiff, while knowing that injury is likely to occur, and
injury in fact does occur:
Pro
‑
Sys
Consultants Ltd. v. Microsoft Corporation,
2013 SCC 57

at paras.
74-83
.

The plaintiff does not plead any agreement to
injure or to use unlawful means, nor does he (if the latter is intended to be
pleaded) allege any material facts related to knowledge that injury is likely.

[
48
]

In terms of negligence, in addition to
misrepresentation the plaintiff alleges that “[t]he Departmental Graduate
Studies Committee of the Pharmacology Department negligently required the
plaintiff to either write his PhD thesis as a master’s thesis or voluntarily
withdraw from the PhD program.”  No material facts are pleaded regarding the
standard of care or how it was breached.

[
49
]

In addition to being confusing and failing to
plead material facts capable of constituting an element of the various causes
of action, the claims constitute a collateral attack on the university appeal
process.  The first order sought under each of the plaintiff’s nine claims is
“an order to void the Master degree obtained in May 2008 with
rescission”.  The plaintiff refers repeatedly to forged and fraudulent evidence
being used in this process.  He also says the University breached its statutes
and regulations by requiring that he transfer from the PhD program to the
master’s program, and that the Senate Appeal Committee decision was tainted by
alleged forgery.  If there were fraudulent documents that materially affected
his appeal, the proper route was to either seek a reconsideration on the basis
of the limited equitable jurisdiction tribunals may have in such circumstances,
or to seek judicial review:
Chandler v. Alberta Association of Architects
,

1989 CanLII 41 (SCC)
, [1989] 2 S.C.R. 848;
Zutter v. British Columbia (Council of Human Rights)
(1995),

1995 CanLII 1234 (BC CA)
, 3 B.C.L.R. (3d) 321, leave to appeal to SCC ref’d [1995] S.C.C.A. No. 243;

Demings v. Workers’ Compensation Appeal Tribunal
,
2012 BCSC 475
.

[
50
]

The plaintiff has been informed of these defects
multiple times, both by this Court and by counsel for the defendants.  He has
been encouraged, forcefully, to seek legal advice.  While he has reduced the
page count of his pleadings, he has not made any progress in remedying their
defects.

[
51
]

In my view, at this point the pleadings
constitute an abuse of process and ought to be struck on that basis.  The
plaintiff will be required to seek leave of the Court should he wish to file
any further claims against the defendants.

“The Honourable Mr. Justice Masuhara”
